---
title: "Writing ANS questions as text files"
subtitle: "Examples and tools for building an ANS question bank with R/exams"
author: "Johnny van Doorn"
date: "22 October 2026"
---

This folder shows how we write questions for **ANS** at the Psychology department of the
University of Amsterdam. Each question is a small text file. A builder turns a folder of these
files into one package, and ANS imports that package with the parts that normally take hand work
already in place, such as **model answers**, **grading criteria** for open questions, numeric
fill-in gaps with a margin, multi-part exercises, data files and maths.

Why files instead of the ANS editor? Questions in files can be searched, reused, compared across
years and checked. Every key in the examples below was recomputed from the data, and a coding
agent can read and write the files too. Everything here was settled by test imports into ANS in
September and October 2026. Where something is only partly tested, the agent instructions say so.

## Start here

New to all of this? This section takes you from nothing to your first package. If you only want
to see the end result, skip to [Try it in ANS](#try-it-in-ans), which needs no setup at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
One of the handy things about a language model is that you can ask it about itself. Stuck on an
install step, an error message or a setting? Paste it in and ask what to do, or ask how a feature
works. Before your agent runs, any chatbot (UvA AI Chat included) can help you get it running.
:::

### What a coding agent is

You probably know chatbots like ChatGPT or UvA AI Chat. You type a question, it types an answer,
and you copy out whatever it makes by hand. A **coding agent** is the same kind of language model,
but it works on your own computer, inside a folder you give it. It opens and writes files there,
runs programs such as R and Python, reads what comes back, and fixes its own mistakes before it
reports to you. Because it works in your folder, you can also give it highly specific context,
such as your lecture slides, lecture transcripts, literature, exam regulations and earlier
exercises, and it reads them whenever it needs them.

For ANS questions, that changes what you can hand off. You give the agent an export of your
question bank and say what you want, for example "turn these into files and recompute every key
from the data". It does the hand work, and you check the result. It can still be wrong about the
statistics, so treat its output as a draft from a teaching assistant. The builder catches
format mistakes, not wrong answers.

### Which subscription to get

Everything here was built and tested with Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent. It comes with a
paid Claude account (the free plan does not include it). Claude Pro, about $20 a month, is enough
to start; see [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing). The more expensive Max plans only
matter if you hit the usage limits every day. Other agents, such as OpenAI's Codex or GitHub
Copilot, can read the same instructions, but we have not tested the workflow with them.

[UvA AI Chat](https://www.uva.nl/en/about-the-uva/about-the-university/ai/ai-in-education/uva-ai-chat/uva-ai-chat.html)
is free for UvA staff and keeps your prompts within the UvA. For now it is a chat window, so it
cannot work in your folder, but agentic use is expected soon. Once that arrives it becomes the
natural choice, certainly for exam questions.

Whichever tool you use, never give it student data such as names, grades or answers. Also check
whether you may share copyrighted or recorded material, such as a textbook PDF or a lecture
transcript, before you put it in the agent's folder. With a commercial account, also switch off the use of your chats for model training in its privacy
settings.

### Set it up, once

1. Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com), a free editor. Open its Extensions view
   (`Cmd+Shift+X` on a Mac, `Ctrl+Shift+X` on Windows), search for "Claude Code", click
   *Install*, and sign in with your Claude account. (Would you rather not use an editor? The
   [Claude desktop app](https://claude.com/download) runs Claude Code too.)
2. Install [R](https://cran.r-project.org) and [Python 3](https://www.python.org/downloads/) if you
   do not have them yet. On Windows, also install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win),
   which Claude Code uses to run commands and to download this folder.
3. Make an empty folder for your questions, open it in VS Code (*File > Open Folder*), and click
   *✻ Claude Code* in the bottom-right corner to open the agent.
4. By default the agent decides for itself which steps are safe. Until you know how it behaves,
   click the mode indicator below the prompt box and choose *Manual*. It then shows every change
   and asks before most commands.
5. Paste this as your first request.

   > Download only the itembank folder from https://github.com/JohnnyDoorn/teaching-statistics
   > into this folder (the full repository is large, so do not clone all of it). Check that R
   > with the packages exams and jsonlite, pandoc and Python 3 are installed, and install what is
   > missing. Then build itembank/examples with itembank/tools/build-ans.R and tell me what you did.

6. Give the agent its standing instructions. Claude Code reads a file called `CLAUDE.md` in your
   folder at the start of every conversation, so you only have to say this once.

   > Create a CLAUDE.md in this folder that says to read itembank/ans-agent-instructions.qmd
   > before reading, writing or building any ANS question, and that I review every question
   > before it goes into ANS.

When it is done, open `itembank/examples/EXAMPLES.html` in your browser. If you see the twelve
example questions with their answers, everything works.

### What we do with it

This is the loop we use for the weekly assignments and exams in our statistics courses. Each
step is one request to the agent.

1. Export your question bank from ANS (*Settings > Export*, both the QTI 2.X export and the
   Respondus package) and put the zip files in your folder.
2. "Convert the questions in these ANS exports into the format of itembank/examples, one file per
   question, in one folder per assignment."
3. "Recompute every key from this data file and list the questions where the key differs or the
   wording is ambiguous. Change nothing yet." You decide what changes.
4. "Write two tick-all questions about the paired t-test, based on section 9.9 of the book, and
   compute the keys from this data file." Always point it to a source, such as a book section or
   your slides, so it does not make up statistics.
5. "Build this folder with a TEST prefix." Read the preview page it makes, which shows every
   question with its answer.
6. Import the zip into a scratch bank, export it again, and ask "Compare this export with the
   expected file." Then move the questions to your real bank.

A few habits help. Ask for one thing at a time and read each change before you accept it. The
agent forgets everything between conversations except what is in `CLAUDE.md`, so when you settle a
convention (say, final answers in two decimals), ask it to add that to `CLAUDE.md`. And keep exam
questions out of public places; this page lives in a public repository, which is why it holds only
practice questions whose answers are already online.

## What is in this folder

| File or folder | For whom | What it holds |
|----------------|--------|----------------------------|
| `README.qmd` (this page) | you | how it works, how to try it, how to write your own questions |
| [`ans-agent-instructions.qmd`](ans-agent-instructions.html) | your coding agent | the question format, what ANS accepts and drops, and what is verified |
| `examples/` | both | 12 example questions in 3 exercises, the built package and a preview |
| `tools/` | both | the builder (R), the packaging step it calls (Python) and an import checker |

## The examples

Three exercises built on Smart Alex tasks from Chapter 9 (comparing two means) of *Discovering
Statistics Using JASP* (Field, van Doorn & Wagenmakers, 2025). The scenarios and model answers
follow the [Smart Alex answers on discoverjasp.com](https://discoverjasp.com/pages/smart_alex.html),
and the questions link to the data files there rather than shipping copies. Every key was
recomputed in R from those data files.

| Exercise | Smart Alex | Questions | What it shows |
|-----------|------|-----:|---------------------------|
| Spider anxiety (paired t-test) | 9.1-9.2 | 5 | a multi-part exercise with a shared scenario; single choice; tick-all; two numeric gaps in one question, accepting either sign of t |
| Pets and life satisfaction (t-test and linear model) | 9.5-9.6 | 5 | numeric gaps with a margin; a single fill-in gap with its explanation as feedback; tick-all with symbols |
| Backward messages (paired t-test) | 9.9 | 2 | single choice whose wrong options are named mistakes; an open question with grading criteria |

[Preview every question with its answer](examples/EXAMPLES.html), or
[download the package](examples/EXAMPLES.zip) and try it in ANS.

## Try it in ANS

1. Download [`EXAMPLES.zip`](examples/EXAMPLES.zip).
2. In ANS, open a question bank (a scratch bank is safest), go to **Settings > Import** and
   choose **QTI 2.X package (Legacy)**. Not *QTI 3.0*, and not *Respondus*.
3. Three exercises appear outside any folder, with titles that start with "EXAMPLE". Move them to
   a folder if you like.
4. Open them and look at what normally takes hand work. The choice and open questions have their
   model answers, the open question has its grading criteria, some questions hold two gaps (each
   with a margin), and the fill-in questions carry their explanation as feedback.

## Build it yourself

Your agent does this for you, but you can also build by hand. You need R with the packages `exams` and `jsonlite`, pandoc (RStudio ships one) and Python 3.
From this folder, run

```sh
Rscript tools/build-ans.R examples
```

This writes three files into `examples/`.

- `EXAMPLES.zip`, the package to import;
- `EXAMPLES.html`, a preview of every question with its solution;
- `EXAMPLES.expected.json`, what each question should look like after import (for the checker
  below).

| Option | What it does |
|-------------|---------------------|
| `--html` | builds the preview only, which is faster |
| `--title-prefix="TEST "` | puts a prefix before every title, handy for a trial import |
| `--feedback` | gives every choice question its solution as feedback too (practice tests) |
| `--out=folder` | writes the output somewhere else |
| `--seed=N` | redraws randomized questions |

The package in `examples/` was built with `--title-prefix="EXAMPLE "`.

To write your own questions, make a new folder, copy the example that looks most like what you
need, change it, and build the folder. One file per question; the file names set the order, so
number them, and give the parts of one exercise names that sort next to each other.

## Anatomy of a question file

A question file is plain text in the R/exams format, saved as `.qmd` (or `.Rmd`). Here is the
part of the spider exercise with two gaps, `examples/1-spider-c-t.qmd`, slightly shortened:

````markdown
Question
========
Test in JASP whether there is a difference between the mean anxiety for the picture and
the mean anxiety for the real spider. What is the calculated t-value? Round to two
decimal places.

t-value: ##ANSWER1##

Degrees of freedom: ##ANSWER2##

Answerlist
----------
*
*

Solution
========
The test statistic, t, is calculated by dividing the mean of differences by the standard
error of differences (t = -7/2.8311 = -2.47). ... When the same participants have been
used, the degrees of freedom are the sample size minus 1 (df = N - 1 = 11).

DSUJ §9.9, p. 384.

Meta-information
================
exname: dsj-09-spider-c-t
extype: cloze
exsolution: -2.47|11
exclozetype: num|num
extol: 0.01|0
expoints: 0.5
exextra[alt]: 2.47|
exextra[exercise]: dsj-09-spider
exextra[anstitle]: discoverjasp Smart Alex 9.1-9.2 - spider anxiety (paired t-test)
````

**Question** is what students see. Its **Answerlist** holds the options of a choice question, or
one empty line per gap. **Solution** becomes the model answer, and in a choice question a second
Answerlist marks the options, with one `* True.` or `* False.` line per option in the same order.
**Meta-information** says what kind of question it is and what the key is.

| Field | What it does |
|---------|---------------------------------|
| `extype` | `schoice` (single choice), `mchoice` (tick-all), `num` (one numeric gap), `cloze` (several gaps) or `string` (an open question, with the essay fields below) |
| `exsolution` | the key, as `100` for options (1 marks a correct one), a number for a gap, or `-2.47\|11` for several gaps |
| `extol` | the margin of each numeric gap |
| `expoints` | the points; in a `cloze`, the points per gap |
| `exshuffle` | shuffles the options once, when the package is built (ANS can also shuffle per student) |
| `exextra[exercise]` | questions with the same value become one exercise with several parts |
| `exextra[anstitle]` | the title ANS shows; parts of one exercise share it |
| `exextra[alt]` | extra accepted answers per gap, with `\|` between the gaps |
| `exstringtype: essay` | with `exextra[essay,logical]: TRUE`, turns a `string` question into an open question with an essay field |

In an open question, a **Criteria** list at the end of the solution becomes the grading criteria
in ANS (see `examples/3-darklord-b-essay.qmd`). The [R/exams website](https://www.r-exams.org)
documents the format in full, including questions that draw new numbers every time they are built.

## What the builder checks for you

The build stops, with a message that says what to fix, when

1. a tick-all question does not say that at least one statement is true (ANS's correction for
   guessing assumes it);
2. a gap has no label right before it (students miss unlabelled gaps);
3. a question holds more than one answer field, apart from several numeric gaps;
4. the grading criteria of an open question do not add up to its points;
5. the parts of an exercise do not sort next to each other.

## What ANS cannot import

- **A model answer for a fill-in question.** The builder puts the explanation in as question
  feedback instead, the same text for a right and a wrong answer.
- **A separate text block above a multi-part exercise.** The shared scenario ends up at the top
  of the first question, which reads fine.
- **Folders and tags.** Imported questions land outside any folder.

## Our conventions

These are our choices, not rules of ANS, so adapt them to your course.

- The correct option comes first in the file; the build shuffles.
- Numeric answers are fill-in gaps with a margin rather than ANS's own numerical question type,
  because a gap shows you exactly what students typed. In a question with several gaps, the
  builder also accepts the obvious variants of each key, such as `0,035` and `.035` for `0.035`.
- Every wrong option is a mistake you can name, and the model answer names it.
- Every model answer ends with its source (book section and page, lecture slides), for whoever
  checks the questions.
- Keys are computed from the data, never copied from a published answer.
- The question states alpha whenever the answer depends on it.

## Check an import

After an import, export the bank again (**Settings > Export**, the QTI 2.X export and, if you
like, the Respondus package), unzip it, and run

```sh
python3 tools/check-import.py path/to/export --expected examples/EXAMPLES.expected.json
```

It prints one line per check (titles, parts, points, model answers, feedback, accepted answers,
criteria, attachments) and marks failures with `XX`. The check that matters most is that no model
answer ended up in the text students see.
